Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to ask my hon. friend the Prime Minister whether he is able to give any information to the House as to the probable liability which we will incur by the reason of the recent developments in the Commonwealth of Australia with respect to the Pacific cable. It is not necessary for me to recall the circumstances to the House. I refer to those which have been given publicity in the public press. The colony of Victoria, it appears, made certain concessions to the Eastern Telegraph Company and the government of the Commonwealth proposes apparently, in lieu of those concessions, to grant a concession extending all over that commonwealth for a limited period of years. That is, briefly speaking, the position of the 1

matter, as I Understand it, but of course my right hon. friend would be much more familiar than I with the particulars. I understand that negotiations have taken place between this government and the government of Australia with regard to the policy of the latter in this connection, and it would be desirable for us to know what has taken place. If my right hon. friend is not in a position to inform the House now, he can take this as a notice, and give the information at a later day. But we would like to know what communications have taken place and what effect this change of attitude of the Commonwealth of Australia is likely to have on the Pacific cable scheme.

Briefly stated, the position is this : Shortly before the Commonwealth of Australia was formed the government, not of Victoria, but of New South Wales, had made a contract with the Eastern Telegraph Company, which is not, we think, in accord with the undertaking assumed by the different governments which participated in the establishment of the Pacific cable. IVe protested at the time, but when confederation of the Australian colonies came into effect it was too late to overcome the difficulty. The arrangement was made for an indefinite time, but the government of Australia have since contemplated making an arrangement whereby the Eastern Telegraph Company would shorten the monopoly granted them to ten years, but it would be extended, not only over New South Wales, but over the whole continent of Australia. We think that this last arrangement would be more detrimental than the first. It must be evident that if, during ten years, the Eastern Telegraph Company have power to establish telegraph stations all over Australia, at the end of the time they will have a practical monopoly and retain control of the whole business, and thus come in conflict with the Pacific cable. We have protested to the Australian government, and the best information we could give to the House would be to bring down the correspondence, which I will be happy to do at an early day.

I would like to ask the government whether they have any information to give regarding the strike at Montreal ? It may be that negotiations are in such a condition that it may be not advisable for the government to say anything, but if there is any information which they can give, the House is entitled to it. I would like to call attention to the fact that the Mayor of Montreal has said

that, from first to last, he has not had a single communication with the Minister of Labour. The language attributed to the Mayor of Montreal, referring to the hon. Minister of Labour, is as follows :-
Not a word have I heard from him, but J expect however, some news from that quarter to-night. Sir William Mulock's place is right here in Montreal at the present time. He is Minister of Labour as well as Postmaster General, and in a juncture like this should be right on the spot to do what he can to help along the trade of Canada.
I gathered from the debate in the House the other day, that some communication had been made to the government by both parties in Montreal, but it appears that the principal officer of that city has not been communicated with in any way by the members of the government, from whom we might have expected some communications with regard to the very serious condition of things existing there. However, I do not rise for the purpose of making any comments on that, but merely to ask whether the right hon. gentleman has any information which it would be proper to give to the House at the present time with regard to the condition of the strike ?

I think it would not be advisable until some kind of settlement has been reached, to give fully the particulars as to the action of the government with regard to the strike. At the present moment, I have only to say-and I hope it will be satisfactory to my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax)-that the Minister of Labour (Hon. Sir William Mulock) and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prfifontaine) are now in Montreal, having left yesterday, for the purpose of doing what they can to obtain a settlement.

Public works-chargeable to income-harbours and rivers-slides and booms-St. Maurice district-improvements of boom works to facilitate the floating and storage of logs, &c. $50,000.

This vote is to meet the requirements for improvements and additions to the works on the St. Maurice, to afford increased facilities for the descent of timber on that river. These improvements are found indispensible to meet the requirements of pulp mills and other large manufacturing establishments now engaged in developing the great resources in that district.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: Will the hon. minister please tell us what is the revenue from these slides and booms ?
The revenue reported for 1901-2, the last year for which we have returns, was $13,565.48.
What is the amount spent for salaries and other expenses ?
The vote to be asked for this year is about $47,000. I shall be glad to give information in more detail when we are discussing the vote for salaries on this work.
Was there not a revenue to the government over and above expenses?
Oh, no.
How much was the deficit ?
Does my hon. friend (Mr. Wilson) refer to the capital expenditure or the annual expenditure ?
The annual. We want to know how much the operating expenses exceed the receipts.
What is the total expenditure on these slides and booms on the St. Maurice ?

It would be better if this question were brought up in the discussion on the proper item. I may say to my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson) that, as near as 1 can figure, the deficit for the last year would be something like $23,000. In answer to the question of the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart), the total amount expended on the St. Maurice slides and booms has been $1,271,282.

But the slides and booms in every other part of the country pay something over and above the expenses. Here is an expenditure of over $50,000 following an expenditure of $50,000 last year, and there is an expenditure on operating expenses of $23,000.

Perhaps my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) did not understand that this vote of $50,000 is practically on capital account, for permanent improvements. The deficit is on operating expenses, for which there will be a vote later on.
I understand perfectly well. I understand that $23,000 is expended in wages and other operating expenses.
That is the deficit.

And a deficit too?
A deficit on operating expenditure. That

is the most extraordinary statement I have heard for a long time. The total receipts are $13,000 a year, and on that a deficit o.f $23,000, and this on works that have cost on capital account over a million dollars, on which we spent $50,000 last year and for which we are asked $50,000 this year.

The receipts, no doubt, will be very largely increased when the improvements are made. But, under present conditions, I do not think they will be equal to the operating expenses. My hon. friend will see that, as I have stated, over a million and a quarter of dollars has been expended on these works. The $50,000 I am now asking for is reported by the chief engineer to be necessary to put these works in a position to be useful and to keep them from being damaged. With the large amount spent during the past year or two, the work will be put in very fair permanent condition. The question asked by the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson) was as to operating expenses, which are quite separate from this.
What kind of improvements does the minister intend to make with this $50,000 ?

At Point a Trudel: Construction of two mooring piers 40 feet by 40 feet by 35 feet, $7,000 ; construction of 12,000 feet of five ply booms, $11,000; at Ste. Flore ; reconstruction of one mooring pier 30 by 40 by 30, $5,000. At Les Hetres : Construction of a new mooring pier 30 by 40 by 30, $7,000 ; construction of 600 feet of two ply boom, $2,500. At Pointe a Marchesault:	Construction of 450 feet of five ply boom, $4,000. At Point a Bernard :	Construction of a
mooring pier 40 by 40 by 35, $7,000. At Us aux Toutres : Completion of a jam pier 30 by 30 by 10, $1,200. Add for works not yet determined and contingencies, $5,300. Total grant required for 1903-4, $50,000.
The minister finds fault with our asking for detailed information on this item. Will he kindly tell us where we can ask for it ?
I did not find fault, I merely suggested that these answers would be more appropriate under collection of revenue, item 238.

Did I understand the minister to say that there was a deficit of about $20,000 last year ? Perhaps the hon. gentleman will explain a statement made by his predecessor on this item in the House last year when he said:
We made out of these St. Maurice booms and slides $20,000 last year. This is one of the rare works that brings us financial results. We are earning more money than we have spent.

It is true that the records of the department Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
show that in the year to which the exminister was then referring, the revenue was $21,322, speaking for the year 1901-2. We have not the returns for this year. No doubt the revenue this year will be pretty near twice what it was last year. We estimate it will be about $25,000.

I find on reference to the Auditor General's Report, volume 1, page B-316, last year, the total expenditure was $153,012, and the total revenue was $13,000. There was only $50,000 voted last year, or $103,000 less than was expended. There was consequently a deficit of $140,000 for that service last year.
My hon. friend is referring to the year 1901-2.
Yes.

There was a large amount expended in addition to the vote. I think there was a special warrant providing for the expenditure of that large amount on account of the breaking of the booms and a large number of logs being lost, in July of that year.

What is the policy of the government with regard to the construction of these booms ? Is it the policy to build these booms all over Canada, in rivers where lumbering operations are conducted, or is it a policy that is pursued on this river for some special reasons ? Are there any conditions affecting this river which distinguish it from rivers of a similar character all over Canada in which persons interested in lumbering operations have to build their own booms ? Then there is another matter which I think we ought to know something about. We voted last year $50,000, we are spending this year $50,000 more. Are the works of such a character that we may expect to have the government, year by year, coming down with appropriations of $50,000 to $100,000 for this service upon the river in question ? When is this expenditure to end, or is it like the song of the brook, which goes on for ever, though men may come and men may go '! May we expect any finality with regard to these expenditures ? Then there is another matter I do not understand. There was a certain amount of revenue from these works last year, and a certain amount spent for operating expenses. What are they exactly, and what is the net deficit on the operations for the year ? From what the hon. gentleman said, there seems to be a deficit in the operation of these works of $23,000.
Yes, that is about the sum.
We ought to know what the gross revenue is, what the gross operating expenses are, and what the *net cost to the country is, of operating the works upon this river.

There has been no change of policy since confederation with regard to slides and booms. I understand that there are three systems that have been kept up in the Dominion, the Trent valley, the Ottawa and the St. Maurice. On most of the streams,
I think the companies attend to these works themselves. This has certainly been a very expensive work. Since 1867 the expenditures have amounted, as I have said, to $1,271,282. I am informed by the chief engineer of the department that a year ago these works were swept away by flood and storm, and it required this large expenditure to make repairs. There has been a great development in that district during the past few years. I am informed that the improvements made last year, for which this $50,000 was voted; puts the system in fairly good shape. It would be rash for me to say that works of this magnitude, costing over a million and a quarter dollars, would not cost something each year to maintain, outside the operating expenses. However, I may give the information given to me by the chief engineer of the department as to what state he expects this vote will put the works in. He believes, that, without any unusual accident or unforseen occurrence, this amount will complete the construction that is necessary and any vote that will be asked for in future years will be for repairs.
Is this vote which is being asked for now for new construction, or is it for a portion of the repairs that have already been undertaken ?
This is for new construction entirely.
Why is this new construction necessary ?

Owing to the immense increase in the number of logs coming down to the pulp mills. The chief engineer informs me that last season over 3,000,000 logs passed down through these slides and booms. Of course, that would materially increase the revenue for the present year when the returns are made.

Why does not the hon. Minister of Public Works put a duty on the logs coming down so that the government shall be put to no loss from the building of these works as they do in every other part of the Dominion ? On the Madawaska, the Coulonge and every other river on which there are booms and slides provided by the government we get a handsome return from them. This river is the only one on which it would seem that there is an immense deficit. The justification, as I understand, for the issue of the Governor General's warrant was, that a portion of this work was swept away by a freshet which led to the * abnormal expenditure of $153,000. Was that the actual damage done ?
There was really more than that. This $153,000 was all expended in making these repairs.

Will the hon. minister answer the first question I asked him ?
I made the statement that in every other part of the country, the parties who use these booms and slides pay a fair amount for them. I may be misinformed, but I understand that the amount they pay yields more to the government than that which they are called upon to expend. Why is it that a like charge is not made on the St. Maurice, so as to recoup the government for the enormous expenditure they are making in that section of the country ?

My information is that the dues collected are the same on the St. Maurice as on other rivers and that they are the same as are charged by the companies. The reason for the deficit is the large amount expended on these works and the apparently large amount required for operating expenses each year.

It is no explanation at all that the hon. minister has received from the officers of the department to say that the charges are the same as those made by the companies. You charge a man the same for the use of a boom at the mouth of the Coulonge, for instance, where the expenditure is very small, as you do for a boom on the St. Maurice, where the expenditure is large. Why should he pay the same for the small advantage that he gets from the use of a boom at the mouth of a river as he would pay where there has been an enormous expenditure on works like those in the St. Maurice ? Why should you not make a larger charge on account of the larger expenditure ?

My hon. friend knows that these tolls were fixed by Order in Council many years ago and when he, perhaps, was a member of the government. There has been no change made since that time. The point that the hon. gentleman has raised, in view of the large operating expenses, is an important one, and I shall consider it worth my while to look into it, and see whether there cannot be some change made with regard to the tolls which are being charged, although they are now the same as they have been for many years past.

One reason that was given, I remember, when we were in the government, for the dockage or slidage received for the passage of logs down the St. Maurice, was that it fully recouped the government for the expenditure. But, things have changed within the last five or six years. There seems to be a greatly increased expenditure. I am taking the statement of the hon. Minister of Public

Works that was made a couple of years ago, and that was read by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) to the committee that that was one of the few works on which an expenditure had been made by the government which fully recouped them for the outlay.
I would like to ask the hon. minister if he could state the amount of money that has been spent on these works within the last six years ?
I would be very pleased to have the department make up a memorandum of the amount expended during the past six years on these works.
Is it a large amount ?
Yes, it must have been a very large amount. There has been a deficit every year since these works have been commenced between tlie receipts and operating expenses.
How long is that ?
These works have been carried on by the Dominion since 1867, and previous to that, I believe, they were erected by the old province of Canada in 1851.
May I ask the hon. minister if these booms and slides are used for any other purpose than the passing of timber and logs ?
There is no other use that I know of except the passing of logs through.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman why it is that the government has anything to do with this matter ? It is not the custom in other parts of this Dominion to expend money simply for the use of lumbermen. They have to build their own slides, booms and piers in all other sections of the country and especially in the province that I come from. I would like to know why it is that the government is called upon to spend a dollar on these works ?

My hon. friend (Mr. Hale) must know that he is mistaken, notwithstanding the fact that he has been a member of this House for a long time. It is not correct to say that no expenditure has been made by the government in other places in regard to these works. I have explained already this afternoon that ever since confederation there have been public' works upon the Trent, the Ottawa and the St. Maurice. As this work was first started in 1851, I can hardly give the reason that prompted the parliament of that day in undertaking it, but certainly, it has been continued every year since then up to confederation and every year since confederation. I am not Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
prepared at the present moment to announce any change of policy in regard to it. The suggestion made by the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) is one worthy of consideration. No change in the tolls has been made for many years. I could not say offhand, nobody could expect me to, and I do not think any hon. member would take the responsibility of saying without inquiry into the subject whether these tolls should be increased or not, but it is a question well worthy of consideration. Considering the difference between the receipts and the expenditures, it may be well to consider whether a saving cannot be made.
Will the minister tell me whether there was ever a dollar of public money spent in the province of New Brunswick for booms and slides in the interests of the lumbermen of that province ?
I am not aware of any expenditure having been made by the Dominion parliament in New Brunswick, on booms or slides.
Did I understand the minister to sav thet the in,inrno fmm tiiGgg works was Si3,000 a year.
I did not say that. I was asked what the revenue for 1901-2 was and I answered that it was $13,565.48, but that is not the annual revenue.
Is that gross or net ?

Gross. I can give in round figures the gross revenue from 1896 to 1902. In 1896 it was $22,000; in 1897-8, $29,000; in 1898-9. $29,000; in 1899-1900, $16,000; in 1900-1901. $21,000; in 1901-1902, $13,565; and the estimate for the present year will be about $30,000.

Considering the enormous capital expenditure that has been made on these works, and considering the small revenue obtained from them it seems to me that the government should take into their Serious consideration, whether they should not abandon these works altogether. I do not see why we should go on spending large sums of money annually for a work which is of no public benefit to the country, and only for the benefit of private individuals. I cannot understand how such a policy can recommend itself to the country.

I cannot agree to the proposition that the development of that section of the country is not a benefit to Canada generally. I may say to my hon. friend from New Brunswick (Mr. Hale) that although, so far as I know, the government has not built or maintained the slides and booms in that province, yet they have expended a good

deal of money on improving the rivers for flic floating of logs. I think'it was probably in the interest of the country that that was done, and it is recognized that the removing of obstructions and the improvement of waterways for the purpose of developing our natural resources, is a wise expenditure. In the earlier days of the country these works were thought so important that many of them were started with public money.

I cannot understand what justification there can be for an expenditure which is only in the interest of the private individuals upon these rivers. Why should the public be asked to pay out money for the benefit of private individuals, when the public get no return from it. What excuse is there for it ?

The same excuse as for any other expenditure. When we build a canal or a railway, or even take the tariff, these are all more beneficial to some people than to others, but it is supposed to be for the general benefit of the country. The maintenance of these slides and booms are supposed to be one of the most useful works carried on by the Dominion for the benefit of the district in which they are situated. I am not prepared to say that some changes should not be made. That matter will have my consideration. We could perhaps make the operating expenses less, or as has been suggested by the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) there might be a change in the tolls which would make the annual expenditure and revenue come closer together. I am not prepared to say that something in that direction may not be done, but I do not think that at the, present time the country would be prepared to endorse the abandonment of these important works altogether, unless they are taken over by companies as they have been on some of the other important streams.
It seems to me that it is a provincial matter altogether. Has the minister considered the question of handing over these works in the provinces ?

While it is true that there has been a small amount of money expended on the rivers of New Brunswick for improving navigation, it is also true that no Dominion money has been expended on these rivers for the purpose of assisting the lumbermen to drive their logs.

The gross revenue was 813.000 last fiscal year, and the minister is taking an appropriation of $47,000 this year for the actual expenses of the staff in operating these works. Therefore we only realize less than one-third our annual expenditure. In addition there has been spent on capital account for the last four years including this year, a sum of $170,000-or at
least we made appropriations for that amount. We have expended all this money on a concern which is repaying us only about one-third of our annual expenditure for operating it.

The minister lias given us a statement of the gross revenue each year since 1896 ; would he be good enough to give us a statement of the annual expenditure each year since 1896. Can he also inform me whether or not in the total expenditure of $1,280,000 he includes the amount for operating expenses as well as the capital expenditure so called?

The total expenditure for construction from 1867 to the 30th of June is $508,956.86, and the total expenditure for repairs, staff, and maintenance for the same period is $762.515.29, making a total expenditure of $1, 271,471.
What about the other question which I asked the hon. gentleman ?
I promised to bring down the information as to the expenditure both on capital and on operating expenses since 1896. That I will bring down to-morrow.

Might I ask the hon. gentleman for just a little more information ? I have an indefinite idea of the nature of these works, but I would like the hon. gentleman to give us as full a statement as he can as to the exact purpose they fulfil.

1 have never been myself on that part of the St. Maurice river ; but I understand that at a great many points there are rapids and falls. The slides are for the purpose of floating logs past those rapids and falls, and the booms of course are built for the storing of the logs, so that they should not be lost by those bringing them down from the upper country.

Works of exactly the same kind in the province of Nova Scotia are undertaken by private individuals, even on more navigable rivers than I think this one is. Is this river navigable for any other purpose than the passing of logs ?

A very considerable portion of it is navigable. I could not say offhand how much. I may say that in the province of Quebec these are the only works of the kind which are now maintained by the government. In the province of Ontario the same conditions prevail as in the province of Nova Scotia, with two exceptions. These works are being very rapidly placed under the control of the lumber companies. I understand that on the Ottawa river the companies find that they can operate these works at much less

26S8
cost than the government tolls amount to, and I have had an application lately to hand over to the companies the balance of the works on the Ottawa river in charge of the government. This is the only instance in the province of Quebec where works of this description are operated and maintained by the government.
In view of the very small revenue derived from these works last year, $13,000, will the hon. gentleman tell us how many men the government have employed on them ?
I hope to be able to give the hon. gentleman that information later this afternoon.

It seems to me a distinction should be drawn between the different parts of the works for which this vote is taken. There may be a strong necessity for improving the character of the bed of the river, and there may be some necessity for a public expenditure to provide slides ; but why should the government of Canada provide the lumbermen with booms, which are generally considered a necessary part of the outfit of any company handling lumber V I would like the hon. gentleman to tell us what portion of this money is spent on slides, and what portion on booms.

I must remind my hon. friend that during the years he has sat in this House he has never offered that criticism before. As I have stated already, these works were commenced in 1851, and since confederation their construction and maintenance have been carried on just as they are at present. While I am willing to admit that the operating expenses are a fair subject of criticism, I am unable to announce at the present moment any change of policy in regard to their maintenance.

I know numerous instances in the province of Nova Scotia in which lumbermen operating on navigable rivers are obliged not only to make the booms, but to buy land on each side of the river for this purpose. It may be that the importance of the lumbering industry on this river makes some difference. I do not know how important it is. Apparently, however, it is not important enough to make this a very profitable matter for the government. There seems to be no good reason why the government should deal with one part of the country in this way, and not with another.
No, it is not. Another rather curious circumstance is that in one year the revenue from the works was $29,000, whereas last year it was only $13,000.

Without dealing in any way with the expenditure on these works, I think it is necessary to bear in mind in whom the property in them is vested. They were created previous to confederation and were the property of the old province of Canada, and at confederation they passed into the possession of the Dominion of Canada, being part of the works referred to in the third schedule of the British North America Act as river and lake improvements. They were taken over and have been dealt with ever since as Dominion property. With regard to the question whether the time has come when we should abandon these works on which so much money has been expended, the question arises, to whom should we abandon them '! Are we going to allow them to fall into decay and become an obstacle to navigation instead of being an aid to navigation ? We cannot force the lumber company to take them over, nor can we force the province to do so. What are we going to do with them ? Perhaps I might say a word respecting the character of the improvements. The St. Maurice river is a very large river on which large lumbering operations have heretofore been carried on. It was at one time the centre of the manufacture of large quantities of pine. Of course the pine has all disappeared, and for a number of years these works were not looked upon as of very great value, and did not produce very great results, but since spruce lumber has gone up in price, these works have become of greater value, as there is a great number of spruce limits on the river. In order to drive the logs, they must pass two of the biggest falls of the Dominion, one which is the Shaw-enegan. It is impossible to drive down these falls, so that a slide is erected at that particular point for the purpose of avoiding the falls. That is absolutely necessary in order that the logs may reach safely the mouth of the St. Maurice, which empties into the St. Lawrence. In driving the logs, you have not only to pass the Shawenegan Falls, but also the Tuque Falls. 1 think that some hon. gentlemen have seen the Shawenegan Falls and would know how impossible it would be for logs to come down them. It is to enable that river to be used for the purpose of lumbering that these slides and booms were built. The booms are not the usual booms used by lumbermen, but are booms to collect the logs at the head and at the foot of the falls, where they are gathered together and driven down the next slide. I may say that there is no other river in our province, except the Saguenay, on which there are slides built by the government. The slides on the Saguenay were formerly built by the government but abandoned years ago and taken over by the firm of Price, Bros., who then had a practical monopoly of the lumber industry on that river. At present

no other slides are maintained in the province of Quebec by the government except those I have mentioned.
Where do these logs float to ?

Down to the mouth of the River St. Maurice, which empties into the St. Lawrence immediately below Three Rivers. At that point there are some of the largest lumber mills of the country. It is known as Three Rivers, because the St. Maurice has three mouths there through which it empties into the St. Lawrence. The pulp mills are above the Shawenegan Falls. The point I wanted to make is that these slides, so far as my knowledge goes, became the property of the Dominion at confederation. We assumed control over them, and I fail to see how it is possible for us to abandon them.
The other' evening we passed an item of $100,000 for improvements at Three Rivers, and I understood that that item had something to do with the river down which these logs are floated.
That $100,000 was for wharfs on the St. Lawrence and these slides are on the St. Maurice.

Then none of this $100,000 is to be spent on the St. Maurice at all ?
Tlie< MINISTER OF JUSTICE. No, the slides are a long way up.
If the government were willing to sell the booms and slides, would they be allowed to do so ?
Parliament could give the government authority.
Then I would advise the government to sell them as quickly as possible or to give them away.
In the case of settlers coming in to| take up waste lands and cut logs, do they enjoy the same privilege as lumbermen ?
Every one is on equal terms. The tolls are fixed by Order in Council.

Are not the booms used for these slides In the same condition as the booms on the Ottawa-specially for the benefit of lumbermen and nobody else. I cannot see why the same principle should apply now as in years gone by. In my younger days, lumber consisted of square timber.
There is no square timber now on the St. Maurice.

Therefore the circumstances have changed, and the same principles do not apply. The slides were built to allow square timber to come down, and it was necessary to have slides. But I 85
venture the assertion that there is no demand for them now for square timber. The booms were built-specially for the benefit of lumbermen who were floating down logs. The logs come down altogether, and when they reach a certain place they are stopped by booms and collected by their different owners. While I would not have the slightest hesitation in supporting any expenditure for the benefit of the public as a whole, I cannot see why we should maintain booms at this enormous expense for the benefit of these lumbermen.

We have much more use for them than before. But the point my hon. friend raises is one on which I have no opinion to express. In reply to my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, I beg to say that the reason why there was less revenue in the year 1901-2, as compared with the previous year, was the very low water which caused the logs to become stranded at various points, so that they could not get down. That will account to some extent for the large increase this year in the tolls collected.
Are the tolls charged so much per log or per thousand feet board measure ?

So much per log. If my hon. friend from Peel would look at page 26 of part 7 of the Public Works Report, he would find a list of employees.
Slides and booms generally, $5,000.

I find that we spenti up to the 31st of December, 1902, $956.96. This was on the Ottawa slides and booms and the St. Lawrence slides and booms and the Gatineau slides and booms. This sum has been voted every year for many years, and sometimes a considerable amount is expended. The year before there were some $3,000 spent, and this year some $700. The expenditure depends on the urgent necessity of the work.
Roads and bridges-Portage du Fort-bridge over the Ottawa-works of reconstruction, provided the Quebec and Ontario governments contribute $5,000, including approaches, $16,000.

This is a revote of $16,000 that has been taken for several years. Negotiations have been going on between the provinces of Ontario and Quebec ; but now the money has been paid over by these provinces under agreement with the conditions on which this vote was given. The plans have been prepared and advertisements are out for tenders.
Has any expenditure been made by the federal government in the meantime ?
No expenditure this year.

Is this an entirely new work, or has a bridge at any time previously been erected at this point across the Ottawa ? Because, it seems to me that the policy of building such works, unless we are already committed to them, is not a very good policy. The provinces of Ontario and Quebec should build their own bridges. Of course, there may be circumstances which justify this.

This bridge was built by the Dominion before. But it was washed away. The provinces of Ontario and Quebec contributed to the original structure, and the same conditions are to be carried out now. Of course, there is no rule or principle laid down for the building of these bridges. We have given assistance to interprovincial bridges in different parts of the country. Prom what I have heard, this is a very deserving case. There is a vote for another bridge, not on the same river, which will come up at a later stage, which also, I think, deserves assistance from this House.
Is this the bridge, mentioned in the Auditor General's Report for 1901-2, page V-320, on which $16,000 has been spent ?
That was for the reconstruction of the bridge at the same place, from the main shore on the Ontario side to Portage du Fort Island.
Is this the same bridge ?
Practically the same. This is for the construction of a bridge from the island to the other shore.

I would like to understand this clearly. In view of the statement of the hon. minister that the contribution of the two provinces have been forthcoming, and that plans have been prepared for the work, 1 asked the hon. minister if any expenditure had been made in the meantime, and I understand him to say none had been made. My bon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) points out that a sum equal to that now asked for, and is described as a revote, has been expended on this same work. The hon. minister.now explains, as I understand him, that this has been a revote from year to year, and that no money has been expended by the federal government, pending the settlement of the question of the contribution by the provinces.
I replied to the question as I understood it. I am strictly correct in stating that no money was expended, but that this is a revote of the total amount. My hon.

friend refers to a bridge which has been built from the shore to the island. It is not the same work as this, but it is practically in the same locality. Until this portion is built, the river is not bridged from province to province. There are two bridges, one from the shore to the island, and the other from the island to the opposite shore. The bridge referred to by the hon. gentleman, that from the Ontario shore to the island, was completed during the past year.
What province does the island belong to ?
The deputy minister informs me that he believes that the island is on the Quebec side.
Then, this is a Quebec bridge.
The Ottawa river divides the provinces, so that this is an interprovincial bridge. Blit the river itself is divided by the island.

I cannot see that exactly. The river between an island that belongs to Quebec and the Quebec main shore is not a provincial boundary. The provincial boundary is on the other side, between the Island belonging to Quebec and the Ontario shore. As I understand it, the bridge from the island to the Ontario side has been built, having been contributed to by Ontario, and now the bridge we are called upon to vote this money for, is wholly in the province of Quebec.

My hon. friend knows that we utilize the island to bridge the Ottawa river. I am not sure as to control of the island, but the deputy minister tells me that he is under the impression that the island is towards the centre of the stream, more on the Quebec than on the Ontario side.

I do not think that makes any difference. Take, for instance, an island in the St. Lawrence. An island on the American side is United States territory, and they have exclusive control of It. We may use the stream on either side for navigation purposes, but the territory is American territory. I think the same principle applies here. I am not finding fault with the expenditure of money, hut if I understand it aright, the Ottawa river is the boundary line between the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec. That river is already bridged. That forms the boundary between the two provinces. The bridge that is to be built is from territory that belongs to the province of Quebec to the mainland. The river is as much a river of the province of Quebec as though it were a river in the mainland. That is the view I take of it. Has Quebec contributed to this bridge that has been built ?
Yes.
When ?
Last year.
What amount ?
Five thousand dollars. I understand the matter as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cochrane) does. But this has been considered in the past as an interprovincial bridge, and it is being treated as such now.
Can the hon. gentleman tell us generally how much has been spent on the bridge during the last ten years, and how much has been contributed by the provinces ?
According to the memorandum I have here the expenditure was $43,098.27. I have not a memorandum of the amount contributed in the past by the provinces for this work.

Does the $16,000 the hon. gentleman is asking for now, cover the expenditure of last year ? Or did he expend $16,000 last year, that amount being supplemented by $5,000 from each of the two provinces, and is he now asking for another $16,000 to be supplemented in the same way ? And, if so, will this complete the work ?
motion from the department is that no further appropriation is required for that work, and that this $16,000, along with the contributions from the provinces, will complete the structure.
No, my information is that the estimate of $16,000 is the total amount we are asked to contribute for this work.
But the hon. gentleman expended $16,000 last year.
But that is completed, we are not asking for anything more.

I confess my dullness, because I am not able to understand what the hon. gentleman means. Here is a work for constructing a portion or a whole of a bridge that is considered interprovincial. The hon. gentleman says that a sum of forty odd thousand dollars has been expended on that from the outset; that he is unable to say what proportion has been contributed by the Dominion and the respective provinces; that the $16,000 was expended on that portion of the bridge last year, and $16,000 more is being asked for this year

I was asked what amount had been expended on the old bridge in this particular place where we are now proposing to build a new one, and I said $42,098.27. But l said that bridge was practically out. of existence, and that to be of any use it has to be renewed. I explained that the other portion of the bridge on the Ontario shore has been built and completed. My Sufor-851

can take sucli action as they think fit. I hope the minister will not press this vote. The vote of $1(5,000 was passed last year, possibly, without much discussion, and without a full understanding of the position in which we stood. I understand from the minister that no money was spent on this particular bridge, it was on another bridge that the estimate of last year was asked for. Then we have the matter much mixed; but X certainly understood the minister to say that the bridge for which he is now asking this $16,000 was entirely swept away, and that practically we have no bridge. I do not understand that any construction has yet been entered upon. The money we voted last year is asked to be revoted again. If an expenditure of $16,000 took place last year, in the estimates it would appear that the $16,000 now asked is' a revote of wliat we voted last year. I do not understand that any money has been expended on this bridge, and I founded my argument for a reconsideration of the whole policy of the government on the ground that no expenditure was made last year, that the bridge had been swept away, that nothing has been done to restore it, and that we are now in the same position as if the bridge had never been built at that point. We have uoth-ing to lose by striking this item out of the estimates.
Will the minister tell us out of what vote the money was expended last year ?

I will have it hunted up and hand it to my hon. friend. My hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson) seems to expect me to be something more than human. I am to have a new policy for the old Conservative party and a new policy for the present government in all these matters. If in years gone by we voted $40,000 or $50,000 for a similar work, he seemed to think that the policy was in the interest of the country, that it was all right, when the money was expended by the government he was supporting. Last year we voted $16,000 for this very piece of work, as we did the year before, but for the other half of it. He has for several years found no fault with the policy that has been carried out. My hon. friend seemed to think that building an interprovincial bridge by the old government, costing $40,000 or $50,000, was good policy and in the public interest.
May I ask the hon. minister : Did he think so ?

Yes, I did, and so far as my judgment goes we may differ as to some matters, but I really think, when we look into the conditions connected with this work, we will find that it deserves to get a proper appropriation. There are other appropriations, Mr. HENDERSON.
perhaps, voted in regard to which we may have our own individual opinions, but, in this particular case, I think, taking all the circumstances into consideration, it is one that commends itself to parliament. When you have built half of this work, when parliament has twice been committed to it by making appropriations towards it, and when this is the third time that a vote is asked when the money is really required to be expended, I appeal to hon. gentlemen if it is not a vote that commends itself to our favourable consideration.

There is no doubt that the provinces of Quebec and Ontario have agreed to contribute towards the construction of this bridge, and there is no doubt that the Dominion government has contributed also. But, if the hon. minister will refer to page Y-320 of the Auditor General's Report, he will see that the method adopted by the government for doing this work is very objectionable. In the first place, the hon. gentleman will see that the Berlin Iron Bridge Company received on the contract for the superstructure of the bridge, complete, $13,700. I would like to know whether the Berlin Iron Bridge Company in their contract agreed to put up this bridge themselves and find the labour for that price.	*
The chief engineer informs me that that was the contract.
And did the bridge contractors furnish their own labour ?
Yes.

Now, there is a total expenditure of $16,497.36. The hon. gentleman will please deduct $13,700 from $16,497.36, and he will see that will leave a balance of about $2,700 or $3,000. I want to draw my hon. friend's attention to the fact that we have first an inspector who received $409.95, then we have, for building approaches and foreman, $633.60, then we have a conductor who received $215.25, and then we have three general officials from Ottawa going out to do something around this bridge at $131.54. We have had the department stating all along to this House that they had a number of architects in the department ; yet, we find that there was paid to an architect, or to some person, 5 per cent of the contract price of this bridge for preparing the plans-some gentleman in the Canadian Pacific Railway office in Montreal. If this method is to be pursued in constructing a work that only costs $13,700, it is very extraordinary and some different method ought to be pursued than that. Perhaps the hon. gentleman can explain it away. That is as I understand it from the figures I have quoted.

I find the hon. gentleman's criticism is perfectly fair. The chief engineer informs me that the reason this 5 per cent was paid for these plans was that they would have to employ a special staff for bridges of this description, and they find it cheaper to get an outside expert to prepare these plans and specifications than to have them made in the department.

What is there special about an iron bridge ? I think if you have not engineers who are capable of preparing plans for an iron bridge at this day in our history, you had better ship them and get somebody in their places who are up to date.

1 think it is probably not from lack of qualification on the part of engineers of the department that this work is not done there. There are several engineers in the department, I think, who are capable of preparing plans and specifications for this work.
If the hon. minister is truly honest, was it not from the fact that somebody wanted a job that had not one V

As the hon. ex-minister (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is not in his place to-day, I am hardly able to answer that question as to the motives that prompted him in regard to some of these expenditures. I suppose that all I can do is to promise to try and do a little better in the future.
Are we to assume that the hon. minister is not going to pursue this method of conducting public works in the future ?

That is a very wide question. What I do say is that I will try if possible to make some reduction in regard to these incidental expenses. This is a technical question. The chief engineer informs me that he finds it cheaxier to deal with a work of this kind outside than to deal with it in the department. Although I am responsible as the minister, I do not want to dispute the chief engineer in regard to that. I think that considerable saving may be made in this direction, and as far as I am personally concerned, I will endeavour to see if it cannot be done.

It appears to me perfectly absurd to say that with an expenditure of $13,700, on an iron superstructure we should spend $1,900 for supervising the job. If we have a plan prepared at $000, and two or three superintendents getting $1,500, it strikes me that there is something radically wrong, and that the hon. minister should not hesitate to tell us to-day that he will not only try to do better, but that he will say that this will not happen again. 1 would suggest to the hon. minister that he
should assume the responsibility for this expenditure. The hon. Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick) is responsible. The hon Minister of Justice is just as responsible as the hon ex-Minister of Public Works is for this expenditure. I will not allow the hon. Minister of Justice to shirk the responsibility of the ministry because the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works is not in the House. The ministers are just as much responsible for his conduct when he was Minister of Public Works in the administration as they would be if he were Minister of Public Works to-day. They should not attempt to shirk their responsibility. It would be more manly for them to justify the expenditure instead of attempting to shirk their responsibility by saying that the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works is not in the House. The hon. Minister of Justice was in office when the money was expended. The hon. Minister of Public Works was not in the cabinet at that time, but the other members of the government are just as responsible as the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works.
Why am 1 brought into this thing ?
We want justice.
That is not what you want.

I want my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) to be fair. 1 have stated before that as a member of the cabinet I do not desire to shirk the responsibility, nor do I know that the premier or any other member of the cabinet does. The question asked me was whether this had been given to an outsider for some reason or other, and I said I could not answer that. We have to take the responsibility for the expenditure, and unless a minister acted without consulting his colleagues-even then I suppose the Prime Minister is responsible for his conduct.
Has the money been paid by the provinces ?

1 am informed that the money has been paid over and is now in the hands of the Crown. The arrangement was that each province was to contribute $5,000 towards the whole cost and that money has been paid.
We are paying $32,000 as against $10,000 paid by both local governments. Has the minister given a contract for this work ?
The contract has not been let.

The wording of the item
would indicate that there is some doubt
as to the provinces paying their share.
Tlie money lias been paid.
Which province does the island on which the bridge will rest, belong to ?
I cannot say. It might possibly be a federal island, but there is a recent decision of the Privy Council which might place it in the province of Quebec. I cannot give a judicial opinion on that.

Would not that be a matter for consideration before the bridge is built.
The MINISTER OB1 PUBLIC WORKS. I cannot see that that enters into it at all. Different decisions have been given by the Privy Council as to the rights of the provinces in the ownership of the foreshore and so on, but there is no doubt about this being a navigable stream, and under the jurisdiction of the Department of Public Works.
It is not an ordinary thing for the Dominion government to build this kind of a bridge, and the minister should give us the reasons why the government was induced to build this particular bridge.
I have given a history of the bridge. It was the policy of the old government and it happens to be the policy of this government.

It is no answer to say that it was the policy of the old government. The late government was defeated, I think not for the good of the country. It is no justification for a minister of the Crown to say that he is following this course because his predecessors did. The House ought to know what induced this government to undertake this work.
I did not say that it was the policy of this government because it was the policy of the late government.
You gave it as a reason.

I did not. I said it was a policy that was in existence for a great many years and that it was the policy of the late government. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilson) wanted to make out that this was the first case of such a thing in the history of the country, and I told him that it was not a new thing, that it is a policy which has been in existence for a great many years, and that it was followed by the late government. The principle that governs this was to assist the people of these districts to have a bridge across a river under the control of the government, and which river divides the two provinces.
I am just as wise now as I was before. If this river is bridged

[DOT]
by the Dominion government because it is a navigable stream, does the same rule apply to all navigable rivers. The minister finds fault because I said that he tried to justify this because it had been the policy of the late government and the policy of all governments since confederation. That is no argument for me. The question is whether or not it is right that this should be done, and I want to know the reason why the government chose this particular river to build a bridge over. If it is done in all cases then that might be an answer, but if it is only done in special cases why was this particular stream selected ?
The hon. member tries to make out that I said we did it because the late government did it. I did not say anything of the kind. I said it has been a common practice by both governments.
That is no reason.

I did not say it was a reason, and I am glad my hon. friend agrees with me that it is no reason. The reason is because it is an interprovincial bridge and after consideration it was thought well to give a grant towards it.
Is that a common practice.	*
It has been a common practice.
I understood the minister to say in his previous explanation that this was out of the ordinary.
I did not insinuate anything of the kind.
The leader of the opposition asked the minister to give him the authority under which this money was spent, and the minister promised to do so.

The Deputy Minister misunderstood the question. This money was voted last year and the year before. But what my hon. friend the leader of the opposition wanted, was the vote the money was spent out of in the year 1901-1902. I will have that hunted up and sent across.
Ottawa city-bridges over the Ottawa river, the slides and the Rideau canal and approaches thereto-ordinary repairs, $7,000.

This vote is to provide for the usual necessary ordinary renewals and repairs to bridges in the city of Ottawa and the approaches thereto, the maintenance of which was assumed by the government under Order in Council of the 17th of June, 1885.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us where the Minto bridge is ?
I do not think there is any bridge under the jurisdiction of the department of Public Works known as the Mlnto bridge.
I know that, but I wanted to find out where it was.
The deputy'minister informs me that one of the bridges on the way to Rideau Hall, under the control of the Ottawa Improvement Commission, is called Minto bridge.

I understood that the Ottawa Improvement Commission had no control over bridges. I understood their work was to beautify the streets of Ottawa. I woidd like to know whether, in building this bridge, they have not gone outside of their duties.
I think one of the first works they did was to build the bridges across the Rideau river. Tlie bridges have no connection with the department in any way.
Is the Dominion government responsible for all the bridges over the canals ?

1 think probably the Dominion government build and maintain all the bridges over the canals throughout the Dominion.
Dominion traffic bridges throughout Canada, including approaches, $5,000.
What is this ?

This is for necessary repairs to bridges built by the department in the North-west Territories, &c.
Land and cable lines, maritime provinces, $28,000.

The vote of $18,000 is to make provision for the construction of a telegraph line on the east coast of Cape Breton Island from St. Peter's canal to Louisburg, together with an extension from Louisburg north to Scatarie island lighthouse, and also an extension of the line from Gabarouse to North Sydney. This work is under contract, and this vote is expected to complete the work. The vote of $10,000 is for completing the construction of a telegraph line from St. Peter's to Canso and connecting Port Mul-grave with Port Hawkesbury by cable. This is under contract. Its total cost is $13,900, and the present vote is expected to complete the work.
Who has the contract ?
Cameron, Maple, N.S.

speechtext: Were tenders advertised for ?
Yes.

The disadvantage under which the province of Prince Edward Island has been labouring for a great many years in regard to telegraphic communication is well known to this House. For the last two years, while I have had the honour to represent a portion of the province in this House, I have brought this matter to the attention of the House, and on each occasion I have been promised that the matter would receive attention at the hands of tlie government; but finally we have been humbugged by the government, for the matter has not received their attention, though it is one closely affecting the commercial interests of the province. As on different occasions I have with others, as the pages of ' Hansard ' will verify, pointed out the grievances under which the people of Prince Edward Island suffer in this regard, both retarding their commercial growth and preventing the press despatches and news of outside world reaching them except at great cost-think it unnecessary to deal further with this phase here. The question now is as to the remedy, and I consider the government has the ready means in their hands. I understand that a delegation from the different boards of trade of Prince Edward Island have come here to interview the minister and the government on this matter, and I trust that due attention will be paid to their representations and some remedy provided for the exorbitant rates which the people of Prince Edward Island have to pay for their messages, and for the disadvantage which they are under in having no night service or night rates. I understand that the Anglo-American Telegraph Company are willing either to sell out to tlie government or to reduce their rates to the regular service rates paid in the maritime provinces, and to give a night service, provided the government will guarantee them against any loss. The Dominion government is under obligations to give the province an up-to-date service, and it seems to me that the difficulty could be readily overcome if the government would take it up in a businesslike way. I have here the resolutions passed liy the boards of trade of Prince Edward Island, and the report brought in by their committee. It is quite a lengthy report, but it will certainly put the members of this House in possession of the facts in regard to the situation in Prince Edward Island, and I will therefore take the liberty of using a little of the time of the House to read it:
The adjourned meeting of the Board of Trade to consider the improved telegraph service was held last night. The meeting was a most representative one, among those present being Premier Peters, Hon. D. Farquharson, D. G. Cameron. Montague and other prominent men.
President Messervey occupied the chair and after stating the object called upon P. L. Has-zard to read the report of the committee appointed at a previous meeting to fully inves.i-gate the question. The following is the full
