position has already been made by the Anglo-American Telegraph Company by the letter of Mr. J. H. Carson, the manager of said company to Sir Louis Davies, dated 21st March, 1900, and to Attorney General Peters, dated 25th February, 1901.
These suggestions are thrown out by the committee as feasible methods by which the matter may be dealt with, but they do not commit themselves to any of them. It is for the government to carry out the terms of union, and give the island an up-to-date service. The matter, as I have said, lias been before the House a number of times. When I brought it up two years ago, Sir Louis H. Davies said he had the matter in hand and that it would be attended to forthwith, and asked us not to insist upon communications being brought down at that time. Last year I brought the matter up, and the Minister of Public Works replied :
I have to assure my hon. friends that the government will give their best consideration to the important point which has been raised. It is not the first time that I have heard complaints about the Anglo-American Company.
It is like everything else that Prince Edward Island asks for it has to be brought up year after year, and even then the people's complaints are not really listened to.
The hon. gentlemen who have spoken are right in saying that we have the means of reaching them. Several members of the government will be in Englaad in a short time, and, if circumstances permit, I expect to go there myself. I will try to have a short and interesting interview with these gentlemen of the Anglo-American Company.
And so on. Now, the matter is in the same state, practically, as it was last year.
The present Minister of Public Works has, on several occasions, looked after the interests of Prince Edward Island in a praiseworthy manner. I trust toe will not content himself with merely saying that he will look Into this case, but that he will take it up and (leal with it this session, so that an end may be put to this outrage upon the people of Prince Edward Island.

While I have no desire to detain the committee from the important business now before it, I feel it my duty to make a few remarks on tlie question brought forward by the hon. member for East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey). This question is one of vital Importance to the people of Prince Edward Island. The grievance is one under which they have laboured for nearly fifty years. A monopoly was fastened upon them about fifty years ago, and from that time until the present they have contended against it-without any result it is true. Although Sir Louis Davies, some two years ago said in this parliament that there was no monopoly, that the telegraph service of Prince Edward Island was as free as the telegraph service of any part of Canada, yet the fact remains that the monopoly is still in existence, that the people of Mr. LEFURGEY.
Prince Edward Island are charged additional rates for telegraph messages over the short cable of nine miles between Cape Tormentine and Cape Traverse. I would therefore urge upon the government that every means should be taken to end this grievance. The hon. member for East Prince has read the speech of the Minister of Public Works of last year. Notwithstanding what the hon. minister said, nothing lias been done, and the people are still suffering under the incubus of a monopoly. What aggravates the difficulty is that our mail service in Prince Edward Island is so irregular in the winter season that our merchants, farmers and others engaged in business transactions with the outside world are debarred for weeks from receiving letters from outside the island, or sending letters to outside points. This is all the greater reason why something should be done to redress this grievance with regard to the telegraph system. If we had a fair telegraph service, our business men would be able to carry on tlieir business under more reasonable conditions. Under tlie present system we are charged an extra rate for this cable when we can use it, and tlie telegraph offices are closed from eight o'clock in the evening until eight o'clock in the morning, no telegraph communications being received from the mainland between those hours. It does not need to he said that this question is of the most vital importance to our people. My hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) has read the resolutions passed by the boards of trade in the provinces. As I am aware that a delegation is in tlie city at the present time to interview the government with regard to this matter, I feel it my duty to speak a few words on behalf of tlie people of my province. My hon. friend from East Prince has entered very fully into the case. He has shown that tlie boards of trade, who thoroughly understand the situation have, by resolution, placed on record their views on this subject, representing in this matter the whole of the people in Prince Edward Island from East Point to North Cape-not a very large province, it is true, but I still claim, one of the fairest and finest provinces of tlie Dominion. I trust that the government will take action, and, if they cannot make an arrangement with the Anglo-American Company, will take over the service themselves. Mr. Marconi with liis wireless system has sent messages from Glace Bay, Cap Breton, to Great Britain. If the Anglo-American people have a monopoly of the cable, wby cannot the government enter into a contract with Mr. Marconi to establish a service between Cape Tormentine and Cape Traverse, and so give tlie people the telegraph facilities to which they are entitled. I have only one word to add to what my hon. friend from East Prince said. There are only two of us in this parliament who represent the people of Prince Edward Island, who seek to advance the interest of the people of that pro-

vinee and are ready to voice their wishes. The other members from the island are as dumb as oysters. Even when they are here they have nothing to say, and generally they are not here. We are here to attend to the interest of our constituents, and I ask the government to take this matter of our telegraph system into their most serious consideration.

If I understood the hon. gentleman who first spoke, he said there was a deputation here now desirous of laying this matter before the government. Personally, I have not had it brought to my attention, but I would be pleased to hear what the deputation has to say, and give their representations full attention. I am not familiar enough with the matter to make any promises at the present time.

The minister has given me the book that the leader of the opposition asked for, and I wish now for a moment to go back to the item 137. When parliament granted the $15,000 it was on condition that the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario should contribute each $5,000, those are the words in the vote. Now we are expending another $16,000, and I presume on the same conditions, that the provinces should contribute each $5,000. But the word ' each ' is not in this vote.

Perhaps my hon. friend misunderstood me. The total amount contributed to this whole work is $5,000 from each of the two provinces. My hon. friend thinks that each province should contribute $5,000 now. I understand from the deputy minister that the conditions were that the provinces were to contribute $5,000 each to the whole work, and that would include both branches.

It was not so expressed when, in 1901, parliament granted $15,000 for this bridge on condition that the two provinces should each give $5,000. Now we are giving a vote corresponding with that vote of $15,000. There is no doubt that parliament, in granting that $15,000, did so on the understanding that $10,000 should be contributed by the provinces, making $25,000 for the whole work. Now we are giving $10,000 more, and I presume that the two provinces will give $10,000 again.
If the word ' each ' was put before the word ' provinces,' that would meet the case.

In this particular case, I was under the same misapprehension as my hon. friend. The deputy minister informs me that we have got the money in our hands, it has already been paid over. I have no objection to putting in the word ' each.' But it may be that if we put in yie word ' each,' the
Auditor General might say that was another vote, different from the one we had before.
I have no doubt that parliament, on the previous occasion, gave the $15,000 on the understanding that $10,000 would be put along with it.
I can only give my hon. friend the information I have from the department. The deputy minister informs me that was the understanding.
It was so expressed in the estimate.

I was under that impression myself, but I am now giving the actual facts. There is no use changing it, so far as this particular vote is concerned, because the $10,000 has recently been paid into our hands.

For that reason there should be no objection to putting in the word ' each.' ' The works of reconstruction provided the Ontario and Quebec governments contribute $5,000, including approaches.' That might mean $2,500 each.

The provinces of Ontario and Quebec have paid their money. I think these words should come out, because the condition has already been complied with so far as they have any intention of complying with it. If it remains as it is now, I think the Auditor General will rule that this money cannot be paid unless they make a further contribution, and the minister tells us that is not the intention. So it seems to me these words, to carry out his intention, would have to be omitted.
Would the hon. gentleman say when the money was received ?

I would have to get the exact dates from the department. We are in this position now, that we shall have this vote of $10,000, and the $5,000 from each of the provinces, as cash on hand to carry out the work. There cannot be any dispute.
It would make a good deal of difference if the money had been received before this item was put in the estimates by the council. In that case the word * each ' should be put in.
Since the hon. gentleman has brought it to my attention, I will refer the matter to the Department of Justice.

I just heard the closing remarks of the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett). I do not think there was any occasion at all for such a statement, because the members from Prince Edward Island supporting the government attend very strictly to their busi-

ness. If my hon. friend wishes to make any political capital by making remarks of that kind and having them published in the island press, he is mistaken. It is really not worthy of the hon. gentleman himself. He knows as well as anybody else that we are attending to our business here. I can tell the hon. gentleman that only this afternoon we were attending to that very matter. There is a delegation here now to interview the government, and members supporting the government are working with those gentlemen. I think the matter will be advanced in that way better than by the speeches the hon. gentleman made.
What have you been doing these number of years ?
What were you doing for eighteen years ?
I have no objection to your saying what you please. But get tip on your feet.

There is no man in this House who talks more without getting on his feet than the hon. member for Northumberland ; he is constantly interrupting. We take it good na-turedly, and when anybody else makes an observation, he might as well take it good naturedly.

There is no man in the House who talks more than the Finance Minister and says less. When he talks about the last eighteen years, he was not in this House, lie was controlling a smaller portfolio than the one he controls now, he was discussing the propriety of a dissolution of the union, and of his province going into the republic of the United States. I will not allow the hon. Minister of Finance to criticise my action in this House. I was here before the hon. gentleman was, and I know the history of the hon. gentleman very well. Therefore, I am not going to be lectured by the hon. gentleman, although he is occupying a position that he little deserves, a position which his ability does not warrant.

I am pleased to hear the explanation of the hon. member for King's (Mr. Hughes) in this connection, and I am also pleased to find that he accompanied the delegation, and is using his influence with the ministry. I trust that his influence will be successful, and that with this delegation the hon. gentleman will succeed in getting for the people of Prince Edward Island the telegraph service, which they are so much in need of.
Quebec-to repair and improve roadways and increase operating facilities generally to eastward of Godbout, $1,000.

This is a vote of $1,000 for maintaining roadways in connection with . the lines there.
Mr. HUGHES (P.E.I.)
Belle Isle-telegraph line between extreme ends of island, $5,000.
Would the hon. minister explain this ?

This is a re vote of $5,000 to be applied to the construction of a line between the extreme ends of Belle Isle, carrying it along the ridge in the middle of the island. This amount has been revoted several times. The Department of Marine and Fisheries are undertaking considerable improvements in the lighting there. A new lighthouse is being built, and there is under consideration some arrangements in regard to the wireless system of telegraphy. Until these are completed, I cannot give any further information in regard to this work. This is a very important point in connection with shipping and some arrangement will come in a very short time.
Would it be in order to give some explanation in regard to the Marconi system of telegraphy ?
I am afraid I am not capable of giving any information that would be of any use at tlie present time.
Perhaps the hon. Finance Minister would give us that information ?
The hon. Minister of Finance made the arrangement with the Marconi people and he will be in a position to give us some information in regard to it.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) is hardly correct in saying I made the arrangement. The arrangement and tlie contract were made with the Prime Minister, but, however, that is not important. I really do not think there is anything to say concerning the Marconi business that has not been already given to the public through tlie press. When the government contributed a sum towards the erection of a station at Table Head, Glace Bay, we were assured by the Marconi people that they had every reason to believe that they would have commercial telegraphy established before the present day. They seem to have made a success of it scientifically, and several months ago there was general rejoicing at what seemed to be the complete success of the system. They had been sending some messages, not commercially, but some hitcli has since occurred. We were constantly being assured by them that they were on the verge of success. Scientifically it is a success, but they do not seem to have been able to apply it to commercial purposes up to this time. The last communication we had from Mr. Marconi, some months ago, was to the effect that they expected to engage in commercial business at an early day. We felt assured that they would soon be^ble to engage in com-

mereial business. However, we are not in a position to add anything to what has been stated in the public press. There seems to be some hitch, the particular nature of which we do not understand. All I can say is that they have assured us that everything is going well and that within a short time they hope to make it a commercial success.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: Does that mean as to the actual success of the working of the system, or does it mean a financial success ?

No, it means that we will have commercial wireless telegraphy in operation in a short time. They gave us repeated assurances in a general way that that would happen. But although they seemed to have established it for a short time, something went wrong and at the present time they are not sending any messages, and they are not in a position to do a commercial business.
There is.no doubt that the system is successful ?

There is no doubt that the system Is scientifically successful. They have sent messages, but they do not seem to be able to send them on a sufficiently large scale to warrant them in undertaking a commercial business, so that we have not had any benefit from it so far. But. they are forming a company in Canada for the purpose of 'making their connections. They seem to have every confidence in the success of the system, but the public seems to have been a little anxious in consequence of the fact that they have not yet been so successful as they expected in that they have not been able to undertake a commercial business.

Perhaps the hon. minister will tell us how much the Dominion government contributed up to date towards that system, and perhaps, while he is on his feet, he will make a statement as to whether the government intend to contribute any further sum, if so, on what conditions, and whether they are as hopeful now as when the government made a statement some little time ago in regard to. this system.

Speaking from memory, the full sum which we agreed to pay, $80,000, has been paid. We have made no other arrangements. We do not contemplate paying any sum of money other than that originally agreed upon, which was $80,000. I think I would be justified in saying that we are as hopeful now as at any time. A couple of months ago there seemed to be a general conviction that the thing had been accomplished scientifically and commercially. In fact some messages were sent. We have had assurances from Mr. Marconi that it would be made a commercial success. From everything we have seen of Mr. Marconi we have
very great faith in him. He is a great inventor, and he has assured us that he has perfect faith in the system, and we are hopeful that it will turn out all right.
Will the hon. minister tell us whether the money was paid to Mr. Marconi himself, or to the company in which he is interested ?

It was paid to the Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company, with which he is connected. The contract was made with the company, although the original negotiation was held with Mr. Marconi. The contract was made with a company called the Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company.
Who compose that company ? Are they Canadian capitalists, or old country capitalists ?
It is an English company.
Altogether ?

This amount is called for by the general superintendent of government telegraphs to make provision for renewing fifty miles of wiring of the Magdalen Island lines. These lines were built in 1879, and the system has been damaged by sleet storms. It is calculated that the work will cost $2,000.
Will the hon. minister state what was the sum spent last year 7
The amount spent last year was $1,119.50. The total estimated cost of this work is $4,000. The balance of $800 will be expended between now and the 30th June uext.
Has the telegraph system always been under the Minister of Public Works ?
Yes. Ever since the department was formed.
Was there not some mention made of handing these telegraph lines ewer to the Port Office Department ?
1 never heard of it at all.

Does the hon. gentleman say he never heard of it ? I am not saying that it has been suggested to him personally by any action that has been taken, but I assume that the hon. gentleman is a very careful newspaper reader, and upon that ground I have a shrewd suspicion that the-hon. gentleman has heard of it already.

I suppose I owe an apology to tlie House, but as a matter of fact I seldom read the papers, especially certain portions of them. I am not aware that such a proposal was made at any time, either hi the papers or out of them.
Did the minister hear it through the Marconi system ?

Before we leave the consideration of these telegraph items, I would like an explanation from the minister respecting the great void that appears here under the head of the North-west Territories. Last year there was a vote of $62,700 for telegraph lines in the North-west Territories, and this year that item is reduced by $62,700.
That appropriation was made for work that is completed or which will be_compIeted before the 30tli of June next. ~
Is it intended to carry out some further extensions of thfe North-west Territories telegraph lines in the coming year ?

These representations will be taken into consideration, and when the supplementary estimates come down we will know.

Will this be carried out by the Minister of Public Works ?

When I was in the Department of Marine and Fisheries I advocated that the hydrographical survey should be controlled by one department, and I thought it should be transferred to the other department, because they have an organization of boats and staff which ought to do it better than to have it in the different departments, as it is at the present time. It is not a hydrographic survey, as it is generally supposed, but it is for the surveys made for dredging, and consequently is under the Department of Public Works.

House went into Committee on Bill (No. 62) respecting the Ontario and Qu'Appelle Land Company, Limited.-Mr. McCarthy.
On section 2,
I would like to call attention to the rather unusual terms of this section. It provides that from time to time the paid up capital subscribed may be refunded to the shareholders.
I may tell the hon. gentleman that the last three words of that section, ' or provided for,' were struck out in the Private Bills Committee. Perhaps that may meet his objection.

What does that mean : ' provided that all the; liabilities of the company at the time of any such payment art paid ' ? There may be ninety-nine cents on the dollar of the capital returned, and liabilities not yet accrued might be in existence. 1 do not want, to interfere with the general object of this Bill, but I think the House should protect the creditors.
Mr. McCarthy. The hon. gentleman will see by the first section that there must be enough land retained to answer for the paid up capital and the liabilities.
Nobody can say that the lauds are enough to pay the liabilities. My impression is that the only safety for the creditors is in requiring that the shareholders shall remain liable.

The shareholders will not be relieved. If a shareholder has fully paid up his capital, his liability is relieved ai once. The capital of this company is fully paid, so that there is no liability of shareholders. The directors' liability, however, is still there.

I know that when a shareholder pays up, his liability ceases; but when a company returns to him his money, the position is reversed. I would like to ask what the Minister of Justice thinks of this kind of legislation ? The company might pay back to the shareholders ninety-nine cents on the dollar of their paid up capital, leaving one cent on the dollar to meet a large liability to the public.
Mr. McCarthy. If the liabilities are met at the time the payment is made, then no liabilities exist. Any future liability can only be incurred in respect to the assets then in existence; and if any creditor advances money to the company, he is assumed to be astute enough to inquire what

assets are being pledged in respect of that liability. If that is so, the creditors are amply protected.

As the Minister of Justice is here, I should like to have his opinion of this legislation. Here is a corporation ready to go into business. It may incur liabilities up to to-day; and to-night ninety-nine per cent of the capital may be returned to the incorporators, people speculating or dealing in lands, and the company may go on incurring further liabilities with only one cent on the dollar in the treasury to meet those liabilities.

As I understand, the capital is to be paid off out of the assets of the company, and will be reduced to the extent of those payments, and that reduction can only take place when the liabilities of the company have been liquidated; so that, for any future liabilities of the company, the creditors will have to be careful not to contract with the company beyond its capacity to pay. It seems to me the chief result of this Bill will be to destroy the credit of the corporation.

I have no doubt it ought to destroy the credit of the corporation, because no man would see what his security was. But is it right to create corporations that may be in such a state ? You create a corporation that may have a capital of $3,000,000. The directors may reduce that million dollars capital to $20,000 or $5,000, but how does the general public know that that reduction has occurred ?

The general public is supposed to contract with a company with a knowledge of its Act of' incorporation, and when the credit of the company has been very materially impaired by the reduction of its capital, the general public will be put upon inquiry.

They ought not to be put on inquiry, and we ought not to pass legislation which is very much like the wildcat legislation of the western states, where the public do not know what kind of corporations they are dealing with. This legislation will not only affect this particular company, hut every other corporation in the country.
The explanation given by the parties interested in the Bill before the Private Bills Committee was

Who are the parties interested ?
Mr. McCarthy. Mr. E. B. Osier, was chairman of the committee, and Mr. H. S. Osier explained that this was similar legislation to that obtained in England by the Hudson Bay Company and the Canada company.

Was that a good reason ?
Mr. McCarthy. The hon. member lias insinuated that this is only wild-cat American legislation.
I think it is.
Then it is also wildcat British legislation.
That may be so.

It does not appeal to me in the same way as it does to the hou. gentleman. It seems to me that if anybody wants to guard against a reduction of capital by a company, the first thing he would do would be to ascertain what enactments and power that company has. He is put upon inquiry to ascertain what is its charter and to what extent its capital has been impaired before he makes any investment or enters into any contract with it. It seems to be perfectly clear and reasonable legislation.
Are there any other companies doing business in Canada under a charter of this kind whose charter has such a clause as this ?

I think we have just passed a charter with the same clause in it. Before I could give a positive opinion on a question of this sort, I would have?, to read the Act and do not want to commit myself to any off-hand opinion. But having passed Bill (No. 61) which has a similar clause, we are committed to some extent to the principle. The clause in Bill (No. 01) is identical with the one we are considering.

I do not wish to commit the hon. minister to any definite legal opinion, but the point is a simple one. Perhaps the hon. member from Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy), who has charge of the Bill, can tell us if this company is asking special privileges not granted other companies.
We have just passed a Bill with a similar clause. The matter was discussed very fully in the Private Bills Committee, and Bill (No. 03) and this one are of exactly the same character.

That is not just the point. The hon. member for Simcoe has gone outside of Canada for an example of legislation similar to this, and I ask whether, in any charter already granted to a company, there is the same kind of clause.

The legislation respecting land companies is limited in this country, and this is not a new departure. The business of a land company is of lie-' cessity a winding up business from the time it begins to sell its lands. Our company's Act says that the capital of a company should not be impaired, and there was doubt in the minds of the directors whether they could distribute among companies, the shareholders, the proceeds of the land sold, because the lands are the capital of

the country- This clause was therefore inserted, following the precedent set in the case of the two oldest land companies doing business in Canada, the Hudson Bay Company and the Canada Land Company, whose charters were obtained in England. This was the explanation given the committee, and after full consideration the committee passed the Bill, but struck out the last three words of this clause ' or provided for,' making it thus absolutely necessary that the liabilities of the company should be absolutely paid before the proceeds of the land sales could be divided among the shareholders. It is not sufficient that the company should provide for the payment of the liabilities, but the liabilities must actually have been paid.

I suppose the idea is that the only profits of the company are the proceeds of lands sold and paid for, and the directors could not divide, from time to time, these proceeds without this provision. Otherwise they would have< to retain all the assets of the company and would not be able to declare any dividend until it was finally wound up.

My objection is this. Any man who subscribes to stock in an incorporated company is liable for its debts up to the amount of his unpaid subscription. If lie should get that stock refunded, he ought to still remain liable for the amount of liis subscription just as if he had never paid it. Otherwise the creditors would not know where they are. This Bill does not say anything about the real liabilities of the company, but authorizes to pay over its assets to the shareholders, provided it has settled all its apparent liabilities up to the time of such payment. There is a great deal of danger in this. A man, might get his stock refunded, while possibly the liabilities of that company remained unpaid, and he would not be liable to pay for his stock in full.

What provision will there be to ascertain that all the liabilities of the company have been paid before the assets are distributed ? One answer no doubt would be that the burden is imposed on the directors of seeing that the liabilities are paid up, as otherwise they would be personally liable, but possibly their financial ability might not be equal to meet certain liabilities outstanding.
There is no doubt about the present directors.
I do not know anything about the present directors, but they may be changed next year or the year after.

This is really a process of winding up and it is the same legislation as was granted the Hudson Bay Company and the Canada Company. It seems Mr. McCarthy.
to be the only way in which these companies can be wound up.
The assets of the company are being devoured gradually by the sales of lands.
There are no liabilities really.
The duty is certainly imposed upon the directors of seeing that the liabilities are paid before making this distribution.
There would be personal liability on default, I imagine.
I believe there would be.

House again in Committee of Supply.
Surveys and inspections, ('50,000.
The hon. gentleman has already made some explanations about this item, but I would like to ask about the nature and place of these inspections.

When application is made for a work it

is necessary, first, to liave a survey and inspection made so as to be able to form an idea of the cost of the work. In fact, no progress can be made until a careful survey and inspection of the location have first been made. This applies particularly to the building of wharfs, piers and that sort of thing, where an examination of the depth of water, the kind of soil, and so forth, has to be carefully made, before plans and specifications can be prepared. The list of places is a very long one. A number of surveys were made last year in the various provinces.

In the Auditor General's reports this item has been divided under eight or ten heads. It is very desirable that the minister should tell us now what he proposes to expend under the various heads. The items run from $1,000 to $6,000. I do not like this blanket system of $50,000 for general surveys and inspection. If the hon. gentleman would just tell us the various items of the expenditure, and what lie wants for each place, we would then know hereafter, when we come to inspect the accounts, exactly what has been done under each head.

I am not aware that there has been any consolidation of votes. I think the same amount was voted last year, but of late years there has been an increase in the expenditure for this purpose, on account of the increased number of public works to be attended to. I may say that so far as my personal experience goes, this vote is properly used, and is of great advantage to the country. Many votes have been given in the past before sufficient data have been obtained in the way of a survey and inspection, and in some cases the work would not have been undertaken had there been previously an inspection and survey. I find that during the year 1901-2 over a hundred surveys and examinations were made in the various provinces. These of course are made by men competent to do that kind of work, and their travelling expenses, being included in the item, make it considerable. But that is one of the items that, if properly controlled by the department and expended by proper officers, will be a great saving to the country, and will enable this House to obtain as full information as possible with regard to all these matters.

As I explained before six o'clock, the words hydrographic survey' as used in this vote are a little misleading. It is not the intention of the department to carry on a hydrographic survey in the sense in which that word is generally used, for the# purpose of preparing charts for navigation purposes. These surveys and inspections are made for work that the department is called upon to do, and it would be impossible for me to say at the present time just what applications may come in or what work may be undertaken. The work for the past year of course is shown. Some important surveys will have to he made, for instance, owing to the development of the country in the Lake Superior region, at Fort William, Port Arthur, and these places. I find that in the department we have not sufficient data to work upon in order to award a contract for dredging, for instance. Every application that comes in is considered by the department. I may say that the people of almost any district are entitled, when an application is made for certain improvements in the locality, at least to have an examination and report by the department as to the nature and the cost of the work, so that the government and parliament may know what is required to be done. Without that information we, as representatives here, are quite unable to say whether or not the work should be undertaken. In regard to dredging that is to be done, or works which are to be let by contract, it is impossible to proceed with any degree of discretion unless we first know the conditions as they are revealed by a survey and inspection. My hon. friend will know that there are many applications for dredging in various harbours, and a survey has to be made so as to enable us to know what the depth of water is, and what amount and kind of material has to be removed. When building wharfs, piers, &c\, a survey has to be made. While I could give my hon. friend a list of the places where surveys were made for the past fiscal year, I think it would be impossible to give a full list of the places at which it is expected that we shall make surveys during the year 1903-4, except that I might mention some of the larger works that we are engaging in throughout the province of Ontario, for instance, on Lake Superior ;



then there are many of the smaller places on the St. Lawrence, in fact, almost the whole distance where work is being demanded, on the Saguenay, at points in the lower provinces and at the various ports on the Atlantic as well as on the Pacific ocean. So that, my hon. friend will see that these surveys and inspections are made and reports received from all points wherever applications are made, and that it is necessary to make a survey so as to enable us to decide upon the desirability of going on with the work or otherwise.

The hon. gentleman is asking now $15,000 more than \yas expended in 1901-2 for this purpose. The last vote was $35,000 and he is now asking $50,000. When we look at the accounts of the expenditure under this $35,000 vote we see that, there are various surveys that must have been contemplated in advance. The hon. gentleman must know of a great deal of the work that he contemplates surveying and inspecting during the year. All we ask is that he should give us certain particulars and then if he wants a general sum for contingencies let him add an item for that purpose. The hon. gentleman does that in other matters. He takes an appropriation for repairs here and there, and then a general appropriation for general repairs.

I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) that in 1901-2, to which he refers, there was a vote of $25,000 and a supplementary vote of $10,000 which makes $35,000. That was found insufficient for the work that had to be done. Last year there was a vote of $50,000 which it was found will be fully expended before the 30th of June. It is so reported to me by the chief engineer of the department. Owing to the great increase in the number and importance of works to be undertaken I find it will be necessary for that same amount to be voted for 1903-4. I might give my hon. friend an illustration to show how this work has increased. During the fiscal year 1896-7 the number of works examined and reported upon was 244. During the year 1901-2 the number was 463. and we have a great many more than that for the coming year. My hon. friend will see that the expenditure has about doubled^ the amount expeuded on public works in 1896-7 was $695,438, while in 1901-2 the amount expended was $3,785,000, or five times as much; yet we are not asking double the amount formerly voted for surveys and inspections. In these matters, of course, a minister has to be guided, especially one with the limited experience that I have had, by the advice of the chief engineer of the department.
I quite admit all that the hon. minister says, but the hon. minister certainly does not put this item in his estimates without asking his deputy

precisely what he wants the money for. All I claim is that in this committee we are entitled to ask the hon. minister what he asks his deputy and to get as much information from the hon. minister as he gets from his deputy.

I have given the very fullest information so far as I have been able to obtain it from the officers of the department. I suppose it would only weary the hon. gentleman to read over the long list of places where these inspections were made last year. I have given him the information furnished me by the chief engineer as to his estimate of what would be required for 1903-4. I wish to make a few remarks about the administration of the Civil Service Act. We discussed it early in the session, and there seems to be a great difference of opinion with respect to it, not only as between ministers but as between gentlemen on both sides of this House. At that time the chief question was as to carrying out the provisions of the Civil Service Act with regard to section 15, and the Minister of Finance stated, as appears by ' Hansard,' what he thought was the prac-

tice of the departments under that section. I have since discovered that the Minister of Finance was absolutely wrong in his view of what was being done under these mystical words we see so often in the estimates, ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.' The Minister of Finance told us with regard to section 15, that it was merely a question of the order in which certain routine proceedings took place. We were then discussing a chief clerkship; and although the question may not be strictly within this item, I may as well refer to the matter here as elsewhere.
The procedure provided by the Act is : First, that the deputy head of the department shall report that the officer is necessary for the proper performance of the public business in the department, stating his reasons for arriving at that conclusion,; next, the concurrence of the head of the department in that report; and, third, the salary being voted by parliament. There was a great deal of discussion at that time as to the order of these three events. The Finance Minister laid it down that the order was exactly as stated in the Act, in which I entirely concur with him. If that order were carried out, and it were represented to this House that it was being carried out, we would have nothing to complain of. Everybody knows that the deputy head of the department occupies not only a very responsible position; but one in which he is protected by the state. He can only be removed in a particular way, and he is an officer on whom we can rely, owing to the independence of his position. Therefore, under the Civil Service Act he must initiate expenditure of this kind by recommending the creation of the chief clerkship and the several other officers mentioned. Now, I wish to refer to some matters bearing on this subject which appear in the Auditor General's report, and 1 do so for the purpose of showing that, although the Finance Minister was quite right in his view of the statute, the statute is being utterly ignored by the department. At page 49, Vol. 1, of his report the Auditor General sends to the Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals this request :
I have the honour to request to be furnished with a copy of the report, referred to in section 15 of the Civil Service Act, recommending the creation of an additional chief clerkship in your department.
Such recommendation, as the Finance Minister agrees, was the first step towards the creation of that clerkship. Some time afterwards the Auditor General writes again, because he got no answer. The next step is that the Secretary of the Department of Railways and Canals, Mr. Jones, writes to the Deputy Minister of Justice :
By direction I beg to hand you two letters from the Auditor General, dated respectively the 3rd and 12th instant, and also a memorandum from the office of the law clerk of this de-

partment, all bearing upon the promotion of Mr. F. A. Dixon of this department to the office of chief clerk and the requirements of the Civil Service Act in that connection.
I am to request that you will be pleased to advise whether it is necessary in this instance to comply with the provision of section 15 of the Civil Service Act as requested by the Auditor General.
Attached to that is the following memorandum signed ' R ' :
Memo re attached.-Section 15 of the Civil Service Act reads as follows :-
15. A chief clerkship in any department shall only he created by Order in Council, passed afterfa) The deputy head has reported that such an officer is necesary for the proper performance of the public business of the department, stating the reasons on which he has arrived at that conclusion.
(b)	The concurrence of the head of the department in such report ; and-
(c)	The salary has been voted by parliament.
In schedule B of the estimates for the year
ending June 30, 1903, there is an item :-
' For the promotion of F. A. Dixon to the rank of chief clerk, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $1,800.'
Parliament has thus voted the salary as required by paragraph (c) above, and it has done more, it has waived all the provisions of the Civil Service Act which affect the promotion.
Therefore, according to the contention of the department, when we pass an item in these estimates, with the words ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act,' we xvaive the whole provisions of the Civil Service Act, notwithstanding what the Finance Minister says. Then the matter goes to the Justice Department and there is a reply by Mr. Power, acting Deputy Minister of Justice :
I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter of this day's date with respect to the promotion of Mr. F. A. Dixon, of your department, to the rank of chief clerk.
I understand that the Auditor General contends that the promotion of Mr. DiXon cannot lawfully he made unless a chief clerkship has been created in the manner provided by section 15 of the Civil Service Act, and that an opinion is desired from this department as to whether or not the position of the Auditor General in this respect is correct.
In reply, I beg to state that by the Appropriation Act of last session the sum of $1,809 was granted to His Majesty for the financial year ending June 30, 1903, ' for the promotion of F. A. Dixon to the rank of chief clerk, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act..' I am of opinion that the effect of this provision in the Appropriation Act is, not only to provide the salary for the current year, hut also to waive any and every provision of the Civil Service Act which stands in the way of Mr. Dixon's promotion, the provisions of section 15, as well as those relating to promotion examinations, and I think that the Governor in Council may promote Mr. Dixon to the rank of chief clerk, notwithstanding that a chief clerkship has not been created for the purpose in the manner provided by section 15 of the Civil Service Act.
In other words, we have been passing item after item in the estimates, with these words

attached, ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act,' and the Law Department treats that as waiving every provision in the Civil Service Act. The Minister of Finance told us otherwise. He represented to us- and I have no doubt he said just what he believed was the truth-that the regular order was being proceeded with'; but the Railway Department certainly did not act in accordance with that view. The moment it got the estimates passed, it used these words as a waiver of everything contained in the Civil Service Act. Then, there is a further letter from the Secretary of the Railway Department to the Deputy Minister of Justice :
I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your communication of the 14th instant, by which you report in respect of the promotion of Mr. F. A. Dixon, of this department, to the rank of chief clerk.
In reply, I am directed to say that under date May 20 last, an Order in Council was passed whereby Mr. Dixon was promoted to such clerkship, and it is presumed by the department that that is all that is necessary in the matter.
Be pleased to advise if that is the case.
So that although there is an Act of parliament saying that this thing shall not be done until the first step is taken by the deputy head of the department recommending the chief clerkship, yet, by passing these estimates with these few words attached, we have been waiving the whole Civil Service Act without knowing that we were doing so. For that reason I think parliament is bound to be a little careful about the wording of the estimates.

I quite agree with the hon. gentleman that we ought to give careful attention to these words, and see what they mean in each case. Every Act of parliament is capable of being amended, and when we introduce into the Supply Bill the words, ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act,' undoubtedly to the extent of these words, and in the case to which they refer, we amend the Civil Service Act, and we must be prepared in every case to give a good reason for doing so. I think that the statement I made in the former discussion as to the general practice and policy was correct, but there may be exceptional cases, such as the one referred to, in which the Act must'be,departed from. As to the particular item, it is for the 'salaries of engineers, draughtsmen and clerks, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.' These officials do not come under the provisions of the Civil Service Act as to classification. There is no question in their case of promotion to any particular grade in the civil service. They are technical officers, they have no special rank in the service, and they have to be treated as technical clerks. If you were to apply to them the provisions of the Civil Service Act, they
could only be paid $400 per year. This does not make any change in their classification, hut solely deals with the question of their salaries. They are not civil service men called upon to pass any special examination ; they are technical officers, and the only object of the words is to enable the government to pay them more than $400 per year. Officers of that character cannot be obtained at that rate, so that the question in their ease is not precisely the same as in the case of Mr. Dixon.

The case of Mr. Dixon; referred to by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) is a most outrageous one. What possible reason was there for repealing the provisions of the Civil Service Act in his case ? Why should not the deputy minister consulted in that case, have first reported that that officer was necessary for the performance of the public service ? How does the hon. Minister of Finance justify the repeal of that provision of the xfct in his ease ? There are* so many of these amendments in the Civil Service Act that we are getting tired of seeing them in the estimates. I have counted up twenty or thirty cases on a single page of the estimates last session, in which that provision of the Civil Service Act was repealed. We cannot possibly follow up every one of them, and the result is that you have an outrageous abuse of the powers of parliament in that regard. There is no possible reason why the provisions of the civil service should not have been carried out in the case brought to the attention of the House by my hon. friend from Hamilton. Yet we have the Department of Railways setting the law at defiance and smuggling this item through the House without any explanation. I say that it was a most disgraceful piece of business. 1 do not know anything about Mr. Dixon. It may be desirable indeed that he should be a chief clerk, he may be a very deserving officer, and no doubt he is, but what I am objecting to is the means taken to violate the provisions of the Civil Service Act without the slightest shadow of excuse. At least I have heard none from my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to-night. I would ask the hon. Minister of Public Works before this item passes, for a statement as to every one of these gentlemen to whom these words may apply, in order that we may fully understand what we are doingr We have made mistakes of this kind in the past, which are now brought to our attentiou by the Auditor General, and it is high time that this House should see that an end is put to this abuse.

There have not been any mistakes. I have differed from my hon, friend in the past in his criticisms of these items, and I do so again. It is true that items of this character appear occasionally in the estimates.
Occasionally ?

I use the word advisedly, for in proportion to the total number of officials in the service, the exceptions made by these items are very small indeed. A year ago I took the trouble to have the figures prepared of the number of officers affected in this way, by the votes; and in proportion to the total number, it was by no means large. It is not conceivable that in a service where there are hundreds of officials, there will not be some special circumstances to justify a departure from the ordinary rules, and it must remain for the minister responsible in each case to explain the departure. I have no recollection of the case of Mr. Dixon mentioned in the Auditor General's Report, and I cannot recall the particular reasons which my colleague the hon. Minister of Railways gave for the promotion of this gentleman. But I have no doubt that the Deputy Minister of Railways was thoroughly conversant with the transaction and a party to it. ; I have never heard of the deputy minister refusing to give the certificate. As appears by the wording of the vote, that certificate was not necessary and was not obtained, and in the absence of auy information to the contrary, we are bound to believe that my hon. colleague had some good reasons for the step he took. We have not this item before us now except incidentally, but I would not like the committee to think that these exceptions are made without special cause. A man may be of exceptional merit, we may be in danger of losing his services, and may find it necessary to give him a larger salary than is assigned to his rank under the Civil Service Act. Would it not be quite proper for the minister, in such a case, to say that he was entitled to a larger salary than the Civil Service Act allows and fo ask parliament to vote that salary, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act ? It is in such cases that most of these exceptions are made. There are not many cases where exceptions are made to avoid examinations. With such cases I have not much sympathy, but I have warm sympathy with the case of a man, in whose favour an exception has to be made on account of his personal qualifications. I nave no sympathy however for that class of item when it is only designed to exempt him from mjdergoing the examinations provided for in the Civil Service Act. I think that we should insist on examinations, but these exceptions are not more numerous than formerly.
How many temporary clerks are there in the chief engineer's department now ?
They are all temporary clerks.

There are permanent clerks, according to the Auditor General's Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
report, but I would like to know how many temporary clerks there are.
There are fifty-one.

Last year there were forty-two, and they have increased to fifty-two. It seems strange that there should be so many temporary clerks in the chief engineer's office. Surely, it is possible to have some of these men made permanent and enjoy all the rights under the Civil Service Act, and thus avoid the necessity of having to come down every session and provide for an expenditure of this kind. Hon. gentlemen say that they cannot obtain the services of a certain class of men without paying them more than the minimum amount of $400, and they therefore ask this additional expenditure every year, but would it not be better to make as many as possible of these clerks permanent ?

The term ' temporary clerk ' is apt to be somewhat misleading. We have temporary clerks who have been in office twenty years. They are practically permanent, but are ranked as temporary. The particular branch of the service referred to is a technical service which does not necessarily require the clerks to pass the civil service examination, so that there is no reason why these people should come under the operation of the Civil .Service Act. Take architects, engineers and professional men of any class, they would not be any the better because they passed the civil service examination, which is imposed on ordinary clerks. These are, for the most part, practically permanent officers, but they have the rank of temporary clerks and are treated accordingly. Though I have not looked up the estimates, I am satisfied that this item has appeared for many years in the same way.

Of course, it has, and that is exactly what we are trying to get rid of. I have in mind now the case of a gentleman who was employed in the department Of the Interior for about twenty-five years, all the time as a temporary clerk. For ten years or more he was in the outside service and for another ten years in the inside service. He did everything he could to have his name placed on the permanent list. But this was objected to. Being only in the temporary service was a source of annoyance to him. He did not see why he should not be on the permanent list, and, when I was referred to, neither did I. I investigated the matter and wrote to the department and tried every way to induce the minister to have the man's name transferred to the permanent list. After a great deal of persuasion this was done. It is rank injustice to an officer not to have his name on the permanent list, if he is really a permanent officer. After he has been in the service ten or twelve years, why

should he be still considered a temporary employee ? The position is a most unpleasant one for him. Should anything occur in a certain direction, he would be beholden to those who came into power to retain him in his position. A man who has .rendered faithful and efficient service should not be treated in such a manner.

I do not know of the particular case to which the hon. gentleman refers, and it may be that his reasoning, as applied to that case, is quite right. But, as a matter of fact, we may have a person in the position of a temporary clerk whom it would not be expedient to have in the regular service.
Why not ?

Well, there are people doing a class of work which does not demand a larger salary than that they are receiving. I know of such cases in the temporary service, persons who are doing a given class of work, doing it well and faithfully; but the work is of such a character that there is no reason for adding these officers to the permanent staff, where they will advance to higher rates of salary than would be fairly proportioned to the work they are doing. I am not sure that we may not find it necessary to have a further classification so as to provide for some employees who are now classed as temporary.

The hon. minister forgets that when officers have been refused their annual increase the reason given by himself and others was that the officers did not merit it. As a matter of fact, in many cases the government did not give the annual increases, notwithstanding the objections raised by the opposition. Well, if the government have control of the annual increases of these officers and can refuse those Increases as they please, there is no force in the argument of the Minister of Finance, for it would not be necessary that these officers, even if put on the permanent list, should receive increases of salary.

That is quite correct in a sense. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) is aware that, while we still contend that the annual increase is not a legal liability, there is moral force in the argument that people expect these increases; and we have taken that view and have granted the increases almost without exception. Once a man gets into the permanent service, he looks for these increases, and, ns a rule, the officers are getting them. But it may be that an officer is doing a certain line of work, and doing it satisfactorily and getting fair pay for it, and yet there may be no reason why he should be in the line of promotion and have an increasing salary.

I do not find that similar eases are treated alike. Perhaps, the hon.
minister can point out why a clerk living in Ottawa who is an assistant draughtsman, who must pass the civil service examination and is appointed to the inside service, is in a different position from that of the man doing similar work residing in New Westminster or elsewhere. The same is true of a paymaster. Whether in the inside service or in the outside service, they perform practically the same duty and, if they have been employed for years there is practically no difference except that one is on the permanent list and receives statutory increases unless he does something to disentitle himself to them, and the other does not. What my hon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) has pointed out is perfectly true. Yet, as the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has shown, by the simple words ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act ' in the estimates, the government take to themselves power to treat these officers differently from others and in a way never contemplated by the law. This came up in another form not many days ago, when I called attention to the anomaly of a large class in the civil service who practically had no status in the service-clerks doing the work of permanent clerks yet not on the permanent list. I can understand exceptional cases, as, for instance, engineers, who do not require to pass the civil service examination, and who are in a class by themselves. But I have pointed out that there are cases in which men are provided for in that way and do not come within the class. I think we ought to have such anomalies corrected, because, as the hon. member for Hamilton pointed out, they involve possibilities of grave abuses.

Of late, we have been considering the question whether we may not be obliged to create another class in which many of these temporary clerks who are practically permanent may be placed. I am not saying definitely that this will be done, but I am only pointing out that the matter has not been overlooked. There are some who are practically permanent officers, although called temporary, who have the same positions as permanent officers except with regard to the name. I confess that I rather sympathize with the idea that they should be put on the permanent list. Still, there are cases where the service can be had at the present rate of salary, and there is no reason why the officers should be transferred to the permanent list. '

I have not heard in the remarks of the Minister of Finance the slightest justification for promoting this gentleman, whom I mentioned, without going through the procedure provided in the statute. I do not suppose the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) is familiar with the facts, and so he cannot justify the action of the government. But I propose to ask the Minister of Railways to jus-

tify this action at the proper time. I would "dike to understand this before we get through with this item.
Application is made by the head of the branch to the deputy minister and he recommends the appointment

I thought I had found the clause, but I am not sure of it

passing an item ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act,' and you follow the provisions of that Act as closely as you can by giving them any salary that you see fit, and keeping them on as Jemporary employees for any number of years.

The Minister of Justice will not regard that as a desirable scheme of legislation.

I do not care. If it is wrong, the fact that it has continued a long time is all the more reason for curing it.
I did not say it is wrong.

It is unnecessary to go over the old ground which I have urged so often, namely, that one branch of the legislature is repealing in this way a provision which has been enacted by both branches. The Minister of Finance will say that we have worked along very well, and found it a practicable. way of dealing with these matters. How many of these men are included under this sweeping repeal ? There is.
They would be subject to the limitations of salary then.
Then that is a most absurd provision.
To get over the examination.
An engineer, for example, could not come in at a higher salary than $2,400, and that will not get the service of a high class engineer.

Would it not be better to amend the Civil Service Act so far as the salary is concerned, so as to get rid of this difficulty of violating it all the time ? We know that in this country you cannot get men of high technical qualifications for small salaries such as have been named. Why should we every year be passing these items ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Servce Act ' when we know perfectly well that we must pay men higher wages than that which the statute provides.

The hon. gentleman should see in the vote we are dealing with now that out of some thirty-two persons employed, ten are persons who are not doing technical service. The hon. gentleman said that they called themselves technical ; I think it is the hon. gentleman who has called them so. We ought to cure that anomaly, first, because it would put the service on a better footing, and next, because it is so easy to class these persons. I agree with the Minister of Finance that there are certain persons that must be employed in the department for which an exception must be made, for example, such as resident engineers in the various provinces. Then they would be entitled to their statutory increases if they were entitled to them by reason of good service. That is the point I am endeavouring to make. If they are good men, they are entitled to get paid for such services as they render, and they should be put on the same status as a member of the civil service. I think the very fact that one-third of the persons employed do not properly come within the vote we are taking now is a sufficient reason why the hon. gentleman should take this matter up.

Every year the different departments come down and ask for additional sums under this head. I would like to have that point made plainer. If parliament grants a vote under this head does that take away any rights or give any rights to the persons for whom the money is being voted ? Can they come in under the Civil Service Act ?
They can not.
That is what I would like the hon. Minister of Justice to explain.
No doubt the intention of the head of the department who introduces an item of that kind is to evade the Civil Service Act by adding these words to the item.

It seems to me that it is clear and simple and there is no necessity for my hon. friend being befogged.

Under the Civil Service Act it is provided that a chief clerkship can only be created by Order in Council. That Order in Council has to be passed on the report of the deputy head and in that report of the deputy head the head of the department must concur. That is the procedure that in the ordinary course under the Civil Service Act ought to have been followed. Nowr, the Civil Service Act is an Act of parliament and the Subsidy Act is an Act of parliament also. The Civil Service Act can be amended by parliament at any time, and it is amended by the Subsidy Act if there is anything in the Subsidy Act contrary to the provisions of the Civil Service Act. In the case of Dixon, he could not have been created a chief clerk under the Civil Service Act except after compliance with formalities I have mentioned ; but parliament, by the Subsidy Act of last year comes in, and creates him a chief clerk and to that extent it amends the Civil Service Act, so that thereafter he is a civil servant entitled to the rank of chief clerk. That is, by putting his name in the item and submitting it to parliament. '

But I do not find his name submitted to parliament.

If the hon. gentleman will look at the statute of last session he will find ' for the promotion of F. A. Dixon to the rank of chief clerk.' There is the name and he is promoted to the rank of chief clerk. We ought to be indebted to the Minister of Justice for warning us that when passing estimates in future we must be very careful indeed about words, lest we are amending Acts of parliament.

I ask my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) to say whether or not in his opinion-for after all, if he will permit me to say it, there are few men

whose opinion I have a higher regard for- in his opinion is not the Subsidy Act an Act of parliament which amends any pre-j vious Act so far as the previous Act is effected by it.

That is (practically amending it. My object in citing the case of Mr. Dixon was to show how the departments were using the estimates in cases of that kind. He has been performing duties in the accountant's branch previously done by the assistant accountant. He is a faithful and industrious officer and we have promoted him to the first-class.

We are only asking for the amount of money we require.

Therefore the Civil Service Act is being entirely ignored by the government.
Now, I want to point out what the Minister, of Finance said in reply to that, and the Minister of Justice will see that hon. members would infer that the Civil Service Act was being complied with in its strictest terms. The Minister of Finance says :

The Minister of Finance in using these words intended this House to understand that every provision of that Act which he said must be complied with was being complied with, and having regard to what the Minister of Railways and Canals had said

I have a recollection of the circumstances. In the first place, I was not explaining the railway estimates; but the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. looking up the Dixon case in 'Hansard' of
last year. His salary was vofe'd in the

first place just as a salary to a first-class clerk. I quite accept the criticism of my hon. friend in the spirit in which he has made it. In either case, since we have done away with the Superannuation Act. I have been inquiring as to the difference between one staff and the other
Is the difference not clearer since hon. gentlemen opposite have reluctantly recognized their duty to keep their contract with the civil service and give them their statutory increases ?
No, I think that under this the minister is responsible for the salaries paid. He could give a statutory increase or more if he wanted to.

But should that, depend on the mere smile or frown of the minister ? Should not the clerks in the service of the country be in a better position than that ? It seems to me that if an officer in the public service is doing good work, he earns the salary he receives. I do not think that is a- proper way of putting it. I have pointed out that there is very little difference between these two classes. The real reason for the position of this class must be the one I have suggested. For instance, you want a draughtsman. Say the salary earned by a draughtsman in the ordinary way of business is $1,000. You cannot hope to engage a draughtsman to work for the department for $400 a year. He does not give a rap for your permanent staff or anything of that kind. If he cannot get the salary that his qualifications enable him to earn outside, he will leave the employment of the government for the position where he can earn more-as they can often do. The intention of the Civil Service Act, no doubt, is good, and on the whole it may result in good. But I know there are many deficiencies in it, and that some departments of the public service are very much injured by it. What I am pointing out is that the only object in taking the appropriation in the form proposed is that in these branches it 'is necessary, in order to engage qualified men, to pay the salaries
that are generally paid throughout the country.

Whatever the hon. gentleman's theory may be, the practice of the department seems to be the common sense and business practice. Not particularly referring to this item, I think I was right in saying that the Civil Service Act is not altogether a good thing for the service, not altogether a good thing for Canada. I have always thought that, and the more experience I have the more strongly I believe it. We have not the class of men in the service that we should have. Mr.' CLANCY. Has not the hon. minister the means of overcoming that ? If he finds a young man in his department who shows

to bottom. I do not think that any part of the surplus could be better applied than in putting the civil service in that position, that would enable men to live as they should in this country.
